candidates.statement: This guidance provides information regarding quality considerations for ophthalmic drug 33 products consistent with the current good manufacturing practice (CGMP) requirements outlined 34 in section 501(a)(2)(B) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) and 21 CFR 35 parts 210 and 211 for all drug products, part 601 for biological products, and part 4 for 36 combination products. 4 For ophthalmic drug products with a United States Pharmacopeia (USP) 37 monograph, this guidance provides information about applicable criteria from the USP. 5 This 38 guidance also provides recommendations to industry on the documentation that should be 39 submitted in the chemistry, manufacturing, and controls (CMC) section of new drug applications 40 (NDAs), abbreviated new drug applications (ANDAs), and biologics license applications 41 (BLAs), including BLAs for biosimilar and interchangeable biosimilar products. 6 The CMC 42 section of NDAs, ANDAs, and BLAs must be included as required by 21 CFR 314.50, 21 CFR 43 314.94, and 21 CFR part 601, respectively. Relevant records and other information that 44 demonstrate compliance with CGMP requirements must be made available for FDA review 45 during an inspection conducted under section 704(a)(1) of the FD&C Act or when requested by 46 FDA in advance or in lieu of an inspection as described in section 704(a)(4) of the FD&C Act. 7

candidates.statement: In general, FDA’s guidance documents do not establish legally enforceable responsibilities. 56 Instead, guidances describe the Agency’s current thinking on a topic and should be viewed only 57 as recommendations, unless specific regulatory or statutory requirements are cited. The use of 58 the word should in Agency guidances means that something is suggested or recommended, but 59 not required. 60

candidates.statement: Ophthalmic drug products should be appropriately designed and controlled to prevent harmful 82 microbial contamination throughout their shelf life and in-use period, which must be supported 83 by stability data. 13 Unit-dose CCSs prevent the hazards associated with in-use contamination and 84 growth of microorganisms between doses that can occur with multidose CCSs that are opened 85 multiple times over the course of their shelf life. Liquid ophthalmic drug products packaged in 86 multidose containers should contain one or more suitable substances that will preserve the 87 product and minimize the hazard of injury resulting from incidental contamination during use. 14
candidates.context: B. Multidose Drug Products 80 If a multidose drug product does not possess inherent antimicrobial activity adequate to preserve 89 the formulation, it should be formulated with an appropriate preservative. 15 Preservatives are 90 critical to ensuring that the multidose drug product remains free from harmful contamination 91 following potential microbial ingress. Such ingress could occur, for example, if surrounding air 92 is introduced into the multidose drug product following administration, if the tip of a dropper is 93 contaminated by a nonsterile surface (i.e., the fluid path is contaminated), or if a contaminated 94 drop returns to the product reservoir. FDA does not recommend using silver sulfate or other silver-containing compounds as a 100 preservative in ophthalmic drug products because of the significant safety concerns associated 101 with applying silver directly to the eye, including argyria (an irreversible discoloration of the 102 skin and eyes) and granular deposits of silver in the conjunctiva and cornea. 17

candidates.statement: Some manufacturers have sought to use a preservative-free formulation for a multidose liquid 105 drug product in conjunction with a CCS design intended to eliminate the potential for in-use 106 microbial contamination. 18 These formulations and associated presentations should afford robust 107 protection for each unit produced to prevent the hazard of injury resulting from exposure to 108 incidental contamination during multiple uses of the product. 19 There are numerous ways in 109 which such presentations might fail to prevent microbial contamination. Any ophthalmic drug 110 product that lacks adequate preservative properties, when exposed to in-use contamination, is 111 especially vulnerable to proliferation of microbes that can pose severe harm to consumers. CCSs 112 must provide adequate protection against foreseeable external factors in storage and use that can 113 cause deterioration or contamination. 20

candidates.statement: Ophthalmic drug products should be evaluated for extractables and leachables from the CCS. 136 Leachables have the potential to interact with the formulated drug product, which could 137 compromise product quality and therapeutic effect. The assessment of extractables and 138 leachables should consider the primary, secondary, and tertiary packaging components of the 139 CCS, including the labeling components. 140
candidates.context: IV. EXTRACTABLES AND LEACHABLES 134 Semipermeable CCSs can, over time, leach low molecular weight compounds (e.g., plasticizers, 142 lubricants, pigments, stabilizers, antioxidants, binding agents) from CCS components or from 143 labeling components (e.g., inks, adhesives, varnishes) into the drug product. However, this is less 144 of a concern for products packaged in glass containers (e.g., biological products). 145

candidates.statement: Because of the variety of chemical species and the enormous capability of modern analytical 207 techniques in detecting trace amounts of chemicals, it is neither practical nor necessary to 208 identify all detected leachables for safety qualification. However, because ophthalmic drug 209 products are applied directly to the eye, applicants and manufacturers should assess compatibility 210 and safety concerns of any potential leachables exceeding the qualification threshold discussed 211 below. The safety assessment should address the ocular toxicity and irritancy potential of such 212 leachables, in addition to systemic safety, as appropriate. 213

There are two reasons for the 256 differences in recommended thresholds compared to the ICH recommendations: First, 257 ophthalmic drug products are directly administered to the eye, and direct, local application has 258 the potential to produce high local concentrations in the eye. candidates.statement: For ophthalmic biological products, degradation products or product impurities can be controlled 281 by specific acceptance criteria at release and under storage based on historical ranges in pivotal 282 clinical trials. However, some ophthalmic biological products include product-related substances 283 (including some that form under storage) that retain biological activity. Moreover, individual 284 quantitation of each of these individual species may not always be technically feasible. For this 285 reason, impurity considerations for ophthalmic biological products should include product- 286 related substances in addition to degradation products and product-related impurities. Therefore, 287 for ophthalmic biological products, specifications should be established for attributes (e.g., 288 charge variant profile) that are known to be reflective of the mixture of product-related 289 substances and product-related impurities. Other impurities, such as process impurities, can be 290 controlled by using (1) drug product release criteria based on risk assessments for each impurity 291 or impurity class (i.e., host cell proteins), and (2) historical process clearance. Applicants should 292 establish acceptance criteria for impurities, including leachables and process impurities, as 293

candidates.statement: The rate and extent of drug release from ophthalmic drug products are quality criteria that may 303 reflect aspects related to formulation and process variants that are important to control to ensure 304 consistent quality. One approach that applicants can consider as part of the quality control 305 strategy for certain ophthalmic dosage forms (e.g., suspensions, emulsions, semi-solids) is the 306 use of in vitro drug release/dissolution testing. Other approaches are also acceptable, such as 307 using one or more CQAs that are sensitive to the formulation and process variants. The applicant 308 should provide scientific justification for how the control strategy will ensure consistent product 309 quality. 310

candidates.statement: All containers of ophthalmic drug products must be sterile at the time of filling and closing and 326 sealed to prevent product use without destruction of the seal. 30 Additionally, ophthalmic drug 327 products that are OTC drugs must comply with the tamper-evident packaging requirements of 21 328 CFR 211.132. If the CCS has a nonretaining tamper-evident ring (e.g., collar or band) to seal the 329 bottle and cap, special care should be taken so that the ring does not detach from the bottle 330 during use, which could cause an eye injury. OTC drugs with tamper-evident rings should also 331

candidates.statement: Applicants and manufacturers should consider the torque specifications for drug product CCSs 344 because some patients may have difficulties twisting off CCS caps that require extra effort to 345 open. FDA recommends that torque be low enough so that special populations, including the 346 elderly, can open caps without undue difficulty but high enough so that caps remain in place 347 during manufacturing, storage, shipping, and handling. 348

candidates.statement: For all topical ophthalmic drug products, 33 FDA recommends that the maximum fill volume of a 361 unit dose (nonpreserved) container be no more than 0.5 mL for solutions, emulsions, and 362 suspensions. FDA also recommends that the maximum fill for a unit dose ointment or gel be no 363 more than 1 gram. Unit dose containers should not be able to be recapped. 364

candidates.statement: For ophthalmic drug products submitted for approval under an ANDA, applicants should 373 conduct a one-time drop volume/drop weight study to determine drop size during delivery or 374 dispensing. The drop size of the generic product should be within ±10% of the drop size for the 375 reference listed drug (RLD) and within the recommended drop size of 20 to 70 microliters. For 376 any deviations from the RLD, the ANDA applicant should provide a justification to demonstrate 377 that there will be a similar number of delivered doses as the RLD. ANDA submissions should 378 include information on the measurement of drop volume/drop weight and testing conditions, 379 such as the number of drops in the container and its holding angle during dosing. 380
candidates.context: b. Dose uniformity of suspension drug products 382

candidates.statement: As recommended in USP General Chapter <771> Ophthalmic Products—Quality Tests, a 384 resuspendability/redispersibility test should be performed for all ophthalmic suspension drug 385 products. For multidose containers, data for a one-time dose-uniformity study (from top, middle, 386 and bottom of the container) should be provided from at least three pilot or exhibit batches to 387 demonstrate that the drug substance is uniformly dispersed and the labeled dose can be 388 consistently delivered throughout the shelf life. Alternatively, applicants may consider providing 389 data from development batches (such as investigational new drug batches) that represent the to- 390 be-marketed formulation to demonstrate dose uniformity. 391
candidates.context: b. Dose uniformity of suspension drug products 382

candidates.statement: Manufacturers of drug products must establish a program to evaluate the stability of drug 396 products and to use the results of the stability testing to determine appropriate storage conditions 397 and expiration dates (21 CFR 211.166). The following stability recommendations should be 398 considered when developing a stability testing program. 35
candidates.context: A. Container Orientation During Storage 401

candidates.statement: The stability of ophthalmic drug products can be affected when they are stored under different 403 orientations. Before conducting primary stability studies, NDA applicants should conduct 404 preliminary development work 36 to evaluate storage conditions in two different orientations—an 405 upright position and either an inverted or horizontal position. Data from this preliminary work 406 should be used to capture and characterize differences in quality attributes, if any, and determine 407 the worst-case orientation. NDA applicants should use this worst-case orientation when 408 conducting stability tests using batches that represent the commercial manufacturing process. 409
candidates.context: A. Container Orientation During Storage 401 35 For detailed information on the stability protocol, annual stability testing, and data reporting, refer to the FDA guidances for industry Q1A(R2) Stability Testing of New Drug Substances and Products (November 2003); ANDAs:

Rather, these products rely on primary stability studies, 412 frequently including process validation batches, to determine storage under real-time conditions. 413 Where interactions between a formulated liquid biological product and the CCS (other than 414 sealed ampules) cannot be excluded, applicants should place stability samples in an upright 415 position and in either an inverted or horizontal position (i.e., in contact with all CCS surfaces) to 416 determine the effect of all product-contact CCS components on product quality. 37

candidates.statement: For ophthalmic drug products packaged in semipermeable CCSs, applicants and manufacturers 431 should conduct a water loss test to assess the moisture transmission properties of the CCS and the 432 protective properties of any secondary packaging used. Where water loss testing is conducted to 433 comply with CGMP requirements, manufacturers should document information on the test 434 methods and acceptance criteria used, and applicants should include such information in their 435 application (see 21 CFR 211.194(a)). 436
candidates.context: C. Freeze/Thaw Study for Emulsions and Suspensions 438

candidates.statement: For ophthalmic drug products that are emulsions or suspensions, applicants and manufacturers 440 should perform a one-time freeze/thaw thermal cycling study to evaluate the effects of any high 441 and low temperature variations that may be encountered during shipping and handling, which 442 could affect the quality and performance of the drug product. 39 FDA recommends this study 443 consist of three cycles, with temperatures cycling between freezing (-20 °C to 0 °C) and ambient 444 (25 °C to 35 °C) temperatures for a cumulative minimum of 3 days. Periodically throughout the 445 study, and at the end of a predetermined number of cycles, the samples should be analyzed for all 446 quality attributes and compared with the control drug product. Applicants that use alternative 447 conditions and durations for their tests should provide a justification for the test conditions used. 448
candidates.context: C. Freeze/Thaw Study for Emulsions and Suspensions 438 37 See ICH guidance for industry Q5C Quality of Biotechnological Products: Stability Testing of Biotechnological/Biological Products (July 1996).

candidates.statement: Critical quality attribute : “Physical, chemical, biological, or microbiological property or 471 characteristic that should be within an appropriate limit, range, or distribution to ensure the 472 desired product quality.” 40
candidates.context: Container closure system (CCS) : For the purpose of this guidance, the CCS includes primary 466 packaging components (e.g., bottles, drug-dispensing tips, tubes with liner, caps), secondary 467 packaging components (e.g., overwrap), and tertiary packaging components (e.g., shipping 468 boxes). 469 Degradation product : “An impurity resulting from a chemical change in the drug substance 475 brought about during manufacture and/or storage of the new drug product by the effect of, for 476 example, light, temperature, pH, water, or by reaction with an excipient and/or the immediate 477 container closure system.” 41
